item.title: Trust Modulates Speech Entrainment: Enhanced Cortical Tracking for Low-trust Speakers.
item.description:
Journal of cognitive neuroscience
Trust is a critical component of human communication, providing a foundation for understanding, information exchange, and social coordination. Much of the research on trust in speech communication has focused on how vocal characteristics impact perceived trustworthiness. However, little is known about how trust in a speaker affects the neural processing of speech. Here, we demonstrate a two-stage experimental framework to study that question using noninvasive EEG. First, participants engage in a trust-building stage, where they play an investment game with fictional characters, each paired with a distinctive voice and trustworthiness level (i.e., frequency and magnitude of lies). Next, participants engage in a story-listening stage, in which they are presented with stories from the same characters. Data acquired from 20 young adults confirm a statistically significant correlation between the perceived and actual trustworthiness of the fictional characters. Cortical speech tracking was quantified using a temporal response function analysis on the EEG data. We found that the trustworthiness established during the trust-building stage influenced the cortical tracking of speech in the subsequent story-listening stage, with lower trustworthiness corresponding to a stronger cortical tracking of speech. Interestingly, trustworthiness selectively modulated tracking strength, with no statistically significant changes in the spatial and temporal temporal response function dynamics.

item.title: Vitamin B12 deficiency, cerebral myelination, and language development: biological evidence from an integrative review.
item.description:
Developmental neurorehabilitation
OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to analyze scientific evidence on the relationship between vitamin B12 deficiency, cerebral myelination, and its potential implications for language development and speech fluency. METHODS: An integrative literature review was conducted using the PubMed, Scopus, and Cochrane databases between August 2025 and July 2026. The search strategy included terms related to vitamin B12, myelination, brain development, language, and speech. Original studies published in English investigating the effects of vitamin B12 deficiency on the central nervous system, neurodevelopment, or structural brain changes were included. RESULTS: Thirteen studies met the eligibility criteria and were synthesized through thematic narrative analysis. The findings indicated a relationship between vitamin B12 deficiency and delayed neuropsychomotor development, impaired myelination, reduced white matter integrity, and structural brain abnormalities identified by neuroimaging. Furthermore, studies investigating the neural circuits underlying language showed that these same structures are essential for language organization and speech fluency, providing biological plausibility for a potential relationship between vitamin B12 deficiency and impairments in these processes. CONCLUSION: Vitamin B12 deficiency may adversely affect neurodevelopment and cerebral myelination, representing a potential mechanism underlying alterations in the maturation of neural circuits involved in language. These findings support the biological plausibility that vitamin B12 deficiency may contribute to impaired language development through disrupted cerebral myelination, although direct clinical evidence remains lacking.

item.title: During natural vision, semantic novelty modulates fixation-related processing in primate cortex.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
We sample visual scenes with short gaze fixations separated by saccades. While low-level integration is known, semantic integration of foveal vision across fixations remains unclear. We hypothesized that the brain responds to changes in semantic information from one fixation to the next, and therefore postulated a neural signal associated with semantic novelty for each saccade. Novelty was measured from different layers of a deep network on foveal vision. Only semantic, and not low- or mid-level, novelty modulated frontal and occipital fixation-related potentials in male and female human scalp EEG during natural viewing of full-length movies (3.4x106 saccades). Intracranial recordings in male and female humans (9.0x104 saccades) and female non-human primates (Macaca mulatta; 3.3x104 saccades) revealed broadband high-frequency activity modulations in scene-specific ventral visual and frontal brain areas only for semantic novelty. This modulation was stronger for movies than static images, and frontal modulation occurred early alongside occipital modulation, suggesting top-down effects. This modulation of fixation-related activity with novelty suggests that foveal representations are compared between consecutive fixations to construct scene representations during natural viewing in primates.Significance statement Primate vision relies on eye movements to sample the world, yet how the brain integrates high-level meaning across these "snapshots" remains a mystery. By combining deep-learning models with massive electrophysiological datasets from humans and macaques, we show that the brain responds to changes in semantic content between fixations, but not low- or mid-level changes. We identified a "semantic novelty" signal that modulates neural activity across the primate cortex. These findings suggest visual processing is not a series of independent glimpses, but a continuous process comparing consecutive foveal information at the semantic level. This work bridges biological vision and artificial intelligence, providing a new framework for understanding how the brain maintains a coherent understanding of a dynamic world.

item.title: Beyond the cortex, early deficits, late recovery: a systematic review of language outcomes and subcortical mapping after awake craniotomy for diffuse gliomas.
item.description:
Chinese neurosurgical journal
BACKGROUND: To evaluate immediate and long-term postoperative language outcomes in patients undergoing awake craniotomy with direct electrical stimulation (DES) for diffuse gliomas in eloquent regions. METHODS: PRISMA-compliant systematic review (PROSPERO: CRD420261342690) of adults (≥ 18 years) with supratentorial diffuse glioma in the language-dominant hemisphere enrolled in both randomised and non-randomised studies of awake craniotomy with direct electrical stimulation and language mapping. Databases searched included PubMed, MEDLINE, Embase, and Cochrane CENTRAL (from 2010 to March 2026). Study selection, data extraction, and risk of bias assessment were performed independently by multiple reviewers using standardised tools (JBI Critical Appraisal Checklists). Due to methodological heterogeneity, narrative synthesis was performed. RESULTS: Ten studies (532 patients enrolled; 55.3% male) published 2011-2025 were included; tumour grade was reported inconsistently, with higher-grade tumours predominating in the larger cohorts and at least 114 patients having WHO grade 4 disease. Early postoperative deficits ranged from 2.2 to 100% depending on assessment timing and measure (immediate post-op: up to 100%; day 7 to week 1: 2.2-22%). Persistent deficits at ≥ 3 months ranged from 0 to 47%. In three studies reporting whole-cohort outcomes with standardised assessment, rates were 0-5.6%. Papagno et al., using 3-month cut-offs, found that 47% of patients with uncinate fasciculus resection had impairment in famous face naming versus 10% with the tract preserved. The general trend was early decline followed by improvement, with most reported deficits resolving by around 3 months. Heterogeneous deficit definitions and inconsistent baseline assessment preclude treating this as a prognostic pattern, and resections involving the uncinate fasciculus were a notable outlier, underscoring the need for systematic subcortical tract mapping. CONCLUSION: Awake craniotomy with DES remains the gold standard for preserving language. Early deficits are common but predominantly transient, and reported deficit rates appear closely associated with the timing of assessment. Persistent deficits assessed at ≥ 3 months were low in most studies, although rates varied considerably with the outcome measure used and with subcortical tract involvement. Subcortical tract involvement warrants systematic mapping. We advocate for the global adoption of standardised perioperative linguistic protocols to improve data comparability. SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: PROSPERO CRD420261342690.

item.title: Differential structural profiles of the hippocampus and thalamus and their cognitive relevance in unilateral mesial temporal lobe epilepsy.
item.description:
Progress in neuro-psychopharmacology & biological psychiatry
BACKGROUND: Cognitive dysfunction is common in mesial temporal lobe epilepsy (MTLE), yet how much the hippocampus and the thalamus each contribute remains unclear. We compared fine-grained hippocampal and thalamic structure and their cognitive relevance in unilateral MTLE. METHODS: We studied 71 patients with unilateral MTLE (39 with hippocampal sclerosis [HS], 32 without) and 17 controls. FreeSurfer-derived cortical, hippocampal-subfield, and thalamic-nucleus volumes were compared using permutation-based general linear models. In patients, 19 cognitive measures were related to volume using covariate-adjusted partial correlations under seizure-referenced (ipsilateral/contralateral) and anatomical left/right codings. Nested additive models tested the incremental cognitive contributions of hippocampal and thalamic volume. RESULTS: Relative to controls, patients showed widespread thalamic atrophy (34 of 44 nuclei in the full cohort, 32 of 44 in each subgroup), whereas hippocampal subfield atrophy was largely confined to HS and no cortical region survived correction. All 48 corrected volume-cognition associations involved hippocampal subfields; none involved thalamic nuclei. Additive models showed that ipsilateral hippocampal volume explained 7.4%-14.6% of cognitive variance alone and explained an additional 6.8%-18.9% of cognitive variance beyond thalamic volume, whereas global thalamic volume did not add significant corrected incremental variance. Preserving anatomical hemisphere linked verbal comprehension and naming to left hippocampal subfields and working memory predominantly to right subfields. CONCLUSIONS: Hippocampal and thalamic abnormalities showed distinct structural and cognitive profiles in unilateral MTLE. Thalamic atrophy was widespread, whereas hippocampal volume was more closely related to cognition and showed additional variation by HS status and anatomical hemisphere.

item.title: What can functional transcranial Doppler ultrasonography reveal about the cerebral lateralization of writing.
item.description:
FEBS letters
Written language is central to modern life, yet its cerebral lateralization remains far less understood than that of oral language. This review synthesizes evidence from five functional transcranial Doppler ultrasonography (fTCD) studies (n = 268; 228 adults and 40 children aged 7-9 years), a method well-suited to studying writing due to its tolerance of natural movement. The linguistic component of writing has been shown to be left-lateralized in right-handers, mirroring oral language, whereas for left-handers findings remain inconclusive. Linguistic processing appears largely independent of whether words are produced by hand or keyboard. The unresolved issue is dissociating linguistic from motor components as writing movements may themselves be intrinsically linguistic. Future research should address underexplored populations and leverage writing as a model for neuroplasticity.

item.title: ERP markers of language processing difficulties in extremely preterm children at 6-9 years of age.
item.description:
Child neuropsychology : a journal on normal and abnormal development in childhood and adolescence
Advances in neonatal care have substantially reduced mortality among extremely preterm children (≤1,500 g at birth), although survivors remain at increased risk for neurodevelopmental vulnerabilities. This study examined event-related potentials (ERPs) associated with print processing and language-related functions in extremely preterm children at school age. Twenty-six extremely preterm children completed a same/different distractor task involving graphical symbols, illegal letter strings, legal pseudowords, and real words. ERP components indexing print sensitivity (N1), lexico-semantic access (N400), and sensitivity to orthographic regularities (late positive component, LPC) were analyzed across two age groups reflecting early reading initiation and reading acquisition stages. Print sensitivity (N1) exhibited typical developmental patterns in both age groups. However, lexico-semantic access (N400) and orthographic regularity sensitivity (LPC) diverged from patterns reported in studies with typically developing peers, suggesting atypical neural responses to linguistic stimuli despite a presumed adequate behavioral performance. Extremely preterm children may display subtle but meaningful differences in neural mechanisms supporting reading and language processing. These findings highlight the importance of early monitoring and targeted educational interventions to support reading foundations and prevent emerging academic difficulties.

item.title: Cognitive impairment in age-related hearing loss: linking brain structure, glymphatic function, and molecular mechanisms.
item.description:
Brain research bulletin
The neurobiological mechanisms of cognitive impairment in age-related hearing loss (ARHL) remain unclear. This study examined multi-level neural mechanisms from macroscale gray matter (GM) structure, microscale glymphatic function, and imaging transcriptomics. Sixty-nine ARHL patients and 76 controls underwent multimodal MRI and neuropsychological assessments. Glymphatic function was assessed via DTI-ALPS index and choroid plexus volume (CPV). Transcriptomic analysis using Allen Human Brain Atlas identified molecular pathways and key genes linked to GM atrophy. ARHL patients showed GM atrophy in right amygdala, left inferior frontal gyrus, and orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), but increased volume in left cerebellum. They also exhibited reduced ALPS index and enlarged CPV. Mediation analysis showed a significant indirect effect of glymphatic function on visual memory via right amygdala volume. Transcriptomics revealed enrichment in axonogenesis, energy metabolism, and protein ubiquitination, with key drivers including SMURF1 and GAD1. ARHL-related cognitive decline may follow a cascade from sensory deprivation to glymphatic dysfunction, involving energy metabolism, protein homeostasis, and axonal remodeling, ultimately leading to degenerative atrophy and compensatory adaptation in specific brain networks.

item.title: Language Experience Modulates Parallel Acoustic and Phonological Processing of Mandarin Tone: Evidence From Mismatch Negativity.
item.description:
Journal of speech, language, and hearing research : JSLHR
PURPOSE: Second-language (L2) speech perception is strongly influenced by prior language experience, but the neural mechanisms supporting this process remain incompletely understood. This study examined how language experience modulates the pre-attentive encoding of acoustic and phonological information in Mandarin tone perception and whether these cues are processed serially or in parallel. METHOD: Twenty native Mandarin speakers and 20 novice Mandarin learners with a tonal first language (L1: Thai) completed a behavioral tone identification task and a passive listening multifeature oddball event-related potential paradigm. Stimuli were drawn from an 11-step Tone 1-Tone 2 continuum with Stimulus 5 (S5) as the standard and Stimuli 1, 3, 7, and 9 as deviants. Deviants varied in fundamental frequency distance (large vs. small acoustic distance from S5) and category status (across- vs. within-category) relative to each participant's own phonetic boundary for the continuum. Temporal principal component analysis was applied to separate early and late mismatch negativity (MMN) components. RESULTS: Behavioral identification did not differ across groups. However, MMN results revealed that both acoustic and phonological factors modulated early and late responses, supporting parallel processing. Native Mandarin speakers exhibited stronger and more sustained phonological effects across both time windows bilaterally. Nonnative speakers showed greater acoustic sensitivity, particularly over the right-hemisphere electrodes, and weaker phonological effects, with reduction most evident over the left-hemisphere electrodes. CONCLUSIONS: The findings show that Mandarin tone perception involves parallel extraction of acoustic and phonological information at the pre-attentive level, with language experience influencing their relative weighting. The neural-behavioral dissociation suggests that tonal L1 experience supports perceptual decisions without fully automatized phonological representations transferred to L2. SUPPLEMENTAL MATERIAL: https://doi.org/10.23641/asha.34925781.

item.title: Disrupting the semantic network shifts activity to domain-general brain regions.
item.description:
Nature communications
Semantic processing relies on flexible interactions between specialized lexico-semantic regions and domain-general control networks, particularly under challenging conditions. Using transcranial magnetic stimulation interleaved with functional magnetic resonance imaging, we investigated acute network adaptation when the left posterior middle temporal gyrus-a core lexico-semantic region-was perturbed during lexico-semantic decisions in 25 healthy participants. High-intensity transcranial magnetic stimulation over the posterior middle temporal gyrus induced task-specific activity increases across semantic control and lexical retrieval areas, as well as remote domain-general regions. Critically, increased local activity at the stimulation site correlated with slower reaction times, whereas greater upregulation in domain-general frontal regions was associated with less disrupted semantic performance. These findings indicate that acute semantic disruption triggers immediate, flexible recruitment of domain-general control areas consistent with the maintenance of task performance, highlighting the brain's capacity to dynamically adapt to interference. Our findings contribute to the current understanding of putative compensatory network-level mechanisms supporting lexico-semantic cognition.

item.title: Linguistic features from constrained spontaneous speech as potential markers of preclinical Alzheimer's disease.
item.description:
The journal of prevention of Alzheimer's disease
BACKGROUND: Language impairment is an early sign of Alzheimer's disease (AD) that may emerge before more obvious cognitive decline. Linguistic features derived from verbal responses to cognitive tests have shown promise for identifying mild cognitive impairment and predicting AD risk; however, their relationships with established AD biomarkers remain insufficiently characterized. OBJECTIVES: To examine relationships between a comprehensive set of linguistic features derived from logical memory delayed recall (LMDR) responses and amyloid status as well as regional tau burden among cognitively normal participants. DESIGN: In this cross-sectional study, we evaluated associations between two types of AD biomarkers (amyloid status and regional tau burden) and linguistic features using covariate-adjusted regression models tailored to each feature's distribution (e.g., linear, negative binomial, zero-inflated beta, and gamma regression). We then used LASSO regression and the Boruta feature-selection algorithm to identify features most informative of biomarker status. SETTING: A community-based subcohort from the Framingham Heart Study. PARTICIPANTS: A total of 238 cognitively unimpaired participants who completed the LMDR test within 1 year before or after tau positron emission tomography (PET) were included. Of these, 228 also underwent amyloid PET and 227 had LMDR voice recordings available. MEASUREMENTS: Verbal responses to the LMDR test were digitally recorded and manually transcribed. We extracted 54 linguistic and paralinguistic features from transcribed responses using natural language processing, capturing lexical diversity and density, syntactic complexity, semantic/information density, and speech fluency and rate. Tau SUVR values were quantified from PET imaging in 5 brain regions (amygdala, entorhinal cortex, inferior temporal [IT], inferior parietal [IP], and precuneus). Amyloid status was classified as Aβ- or Aβ+ using Gaussian mixture modeling of PiB PET DVR values. LMDR total score and participant demographics (age, sex, education) were included as covariates. RESULTS: After adjusting for age, sex, education, amyloid status, and LMDR score, 23 linguistic features were associated with tau burden in at least one brain region. For example, reduced semantic richness, captured by lower uniqueIdeaDensity, was associated with higher tau burden across multiple regions, including the amygdala (average marginal effect (AME)=-0.007, 95% CI: (-0.013, -0.001)), entorhinal (AME=-0.007, 95% CI: (-0.013, -0.002)), IT (AME=-0.008, 95% CI: (-0.014, -0.002)), and precuneus (AME=-0.006, 95% CI: (-0.012, -1.51e^-5)). More between-utterance pauses were associated with higher tau burden in the entorhinal (AME=0.259, 95% CI: (0.026, 0.493)), IT (AME=0.272, 95% CI: (0.025, 0.518)), and IP (AME=0.404, 95% CI: (0.160, 0.648)) regions. No linguistic features were associated with amyloid status, and LMDR total score was not associated with either tau burden or amyloid status. LASSO regression selected 3-7 features per brain region, capturing multiple aspects of language use (e.g., speech disfluency and semantic density) associated with tau burden. The nonlinear Boruta algorithm selected a larger set of biomarker-informative features, including predictors of amyloid positivity, and identified additional syntactic measures (e.g., Yngve score, mean dependency distance) as important predictors of regional tau burden. CONCLUSIONS: Linguistic features derived from neuropsychological (NP) tests capture subtle language changes associated with regional tau pathology in cognitively normal individuals, beyond conventional NP test scores. These findings highlight the potential of language-based measures as non-invasive digital biomarkers for early AD risk stratification and for supporting clinical decision-making about biomarker testing for possible preclinical AD.

item.title: Semantic Similarity-Related Neural Patterns and Their Associations with GABA-Glutamate Levels in the Left Inferior Frontal Gyrus, Anterior Temporal Lobe, and Inferior Parietal Lobule.
item.description:
Biological psychology
It remains unclear how graded lexical-semantic similarity between prime-target pairs is reflected in mean BOLD responses and multivariate neural activity patterns, and how these neural indices relate to regional GABA, Glx (glutamate + glutamine), and GABA/Glx levels. We examined the neural correlates of lexical-semantic similarity and their associations with regional neurochemical measures in 46 healthy adults using fMRI during a semantic priming task and magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) acquired on a separate day. Trial-wise prime-target semantic similarity was quantified using word-vector cosine similarity. Similarity-related BOLD responses were assessed using parametric modulation, whereas neural-semantic correspondence was examined using representational similarity analysis (RSA). Semantic similarity modulated BOLD activity primarily under incongruency, involving premotor, dorsolateral prefrontal, frontal eye field, angular gyrus, and anterior prefrontal regions. ROI-based RSA revealed FWE-corrected neural-semantic correspondence in the left inferior frontal gyrus pars opercularis (IFG-Op) and medial superior frontal gyrus. Within-condition analyses further showed distributed neural-semantic correspondence under incongruency across frontal, temporal, and parietal regions implicated in semantic control and integration processes, including bilateral IFG and the left inferior parietal lobule (IPL). Additionally, a positive association was observed between RSA model fit and left IPL Glx levels in the incongruent condition, although this association did not survive FDR correction. Together, these findings suggest that lexical-semantic similarity is reflected in condition-dependent neural responses and representational geometry and may represent an additional dimension modulating semantic control demands, while evidence for associations with regional neurochemical measures remains preliminary.

item.title: Differential modulation of the neurocomputational signature of early and late mismatch responses to spoken words by awareness and task relevance
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Mismatch responses (MMRs), including the mismatch negativity (MMN) and the P3, are a hallmark of the brain’s capacity to detect unexpected events. They are discussed to be generated by two main processes: adaptation and prediction error (PE). However, MMR research on underlying mechanisms has mostly relied on simple, non-linguistic stimuli such as tones, and it remains unknown how awareness and attentional conditions affect MMRs to auditory verbal stimuli, that, unlike tones, carry lexical-semantic meaning. Here, we conducted a preregistered EEG study that disentangled influences of awareness, general task-relevance of word stimuli, and specific target-relevance of word oddballs on the MMN and P3. In addition, single-trial neurocomputational models were applied to uncover the underlying generative models of the MMRs. Results show that word-related MMN and P3 were only elicited when words were task-relevant, and the P3 increased with target-relevance. Crucially, no word-related MMN emerged under inattention, in contrast to the pre-attentive MMN typically reported for tonal deviants. Neurocomputational modeling revealed that the early part of the task-relevant MMN reflects adaptation processes. PE processes generated later parts of the MMN under task-relevance, and the entire MMN under target-relevance, as well as the P3 independent of relevance conditions. This suggests that the same temporal generation pattern of adaptation and PE underlie mismatch responses to both words and tones, but that, unlike tonal MMRs, eliciting MMRs to words requires the allocation of attention. This attentional dependency may reflect the additional lexical-semantic and multi-level representational demands that spoken words impose on the auditory system.

item.title: Connectivity of Implicit Statistical Learning Networks is Associated with Language Impairment Severity in Post-Stroke Aphasia
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Rehabilitation of language for individuals with post-stroke aphasia (PSA) requires relearning to use cognitive-linguistic skills, but little is known about how these individuals relearn, or how brain reorganization may support different types of learning. One type of learning critical to language acquisition is implicit-statistical learning (ISL), which supports robust, accurate performance with minimal conscious effort. ISL relies on brain subnetworks that include language areas as well as domain general regions (i.e., salience and cognitive control) with the latter considered less likely to be damaged in individuals with PSA. Using three brain subnetworks previously found to be associated with ISL, the present study used graph theory metrics to (1) compare their functional connectivity in PSA (n = 30) relative to neurologically healthy controls (n=18), and (2) examine their relationship with aphasia severity in the PSA group. Resting-state functional connectivity was weaker for the language and salience subnetworks in PSA than controls, but not for the cognitive control subnetwork. Additionally, edges within all three networks correlated with aphasia severity, particularly between regions of the right frontal cortex, such that stronger connectivity in these ISL subnetworks were associated with milder aphasia. While it is unsurprising that the damaged left-sided brain regions in the PSA group resulted in connectivity that differed from controls, these differences were also observed in the salience subnetwork. Further, the correspondence to aphasia severity was evident in all subnetworks, highlighting that domain general ISL networks may contribute to variability in language outcomes.

item.title: Neural connectomes of verbal fluency in post-stroke aphasia.
item.description:
Journal of the International Neuropsychological Society : JINS
Verbal fluency tasks are widely used to assess language abilities and executive functions in both clinical and research settings. In post-stroke patients, prior research has indicated a significant hodological contribution to the neural basis of verbal fluency; however, this has largely been examined using lesion-based measures, predefined tractography approaches, and traditional diffusion metrics. Quantitative anisotropy-based structural connectometry derived from correlational tractography was employed to determine the white matter circuits underlying semantic and phonemic fluency in 44 patients with post-stroke aphasia. Both task types were found to be linked to anterior frontal connections of left-hemisphere dorsal and ventral associative pathways, as well as domain-general projection pathways. However, visual inspection of the connectomes, supported by supplementary cross-control analyses, suggested differences in the relative emphasis and distribution of pathways, with phonemic fluency aligning more with the dorsal stream, while semantic fluency showed greater reliance on the ventral stream and a wider range of cortico-subcortical connections. The findings contribute to current understanding of the neural networks of verbal fluency in aphasia, with potential relevance for clinical practice and research.

item.title: Neural discrimination of emotional prosody in natural sentences in 2- to 3-month-old infants using OPM-MEG
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
From birth, infants are sensitive to the emotional prosody of speech, yet it remains unclear when the developing brain discriminates emotions conveyed by natural spoken sentences. Here, we recorded brain activity with optically pumped magnetometer magnetoencephalography (OPM-MEG) in 15 infants aged 2-3 months while they listened to semantically neutral sentences spoken with happy or angry prosody. Natural sentences elicited robust auditory evoked responses, with prominent components at 88, 216, 380 and 1,356 ms after sentence onset and sources centred on bilateral superior and middle temporal cortex. Time-resolved multivariate pattern analysis revealed that distributed neural activity discriminated recordings spoken with happy from angry prosody 346-454 ms after the onset of the prosodically prominent word (the first word carrying a pitch peak), despite no difference in global field power between conditions. This discrimination was transient, emerged before the end of the sentence, and was carried primarily by phase-locked delta-band activity, followed by later differences in induced alpha power. Angry prosody also delayed the late auditory response by approximately 15 ms with no detectable changes in amplitude. Our findings show that cortical responses to happy and angry prosody in natural speech differ by 2-3 months of age, and demonstrate that OPM-MEG combined with time-resolved decoding can reveal the temporal, spatial and spectral organisation of early emotional-prosody processing.

item.title: A domain-general basal ganglia mechanism for inhibitory control during language comprehension
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Whether controlled language processing involves domain-general or language-specific neural circuits is subject of controversial debate. We tested whether the inhibitory control of linguistic activity shares a common neural process with motor inhibition in twenty humans undergoing intra- and extracranial neural field potential recordings and deep-brain stimulation. Engaging motor and linguistic inhibition simultaneously resulted in a significant behavioral cost, suggesting a shared underlying neural process. Indeed, neural decoders trained during motor inhibition were able to decode linguistic inhibition and vice versa. Depth-electrode recordings from the subthalamic nucleus (STN), a key basal ganglia area for inhibitory control, showed increased β-band (13-30 Hz) activity during both linguistic and motor inhibition. Finally, disrupting the STN via deep-brain stimulation impaired behavioral and neural signatures of both linguistic and motor inhibition. Together, these findings show that the inhibitory control of language and movement share a domain-general mechanism implemented via the subthalamic nucleus of the basal ganglia.

item.title: Hierarchical Uncertainty Transformation During Multimodal Comprehension
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Human communication requires combining information from different modalities even when each source is incomplete or ambiguous. Yet how uncertainty is coordinated as distinct semantic representations interact and converge remains unclear. Here we propose a hierarchical uncertainty transformation framework and test it across four gesture–speech experiments combining behavioral measures, information-theoretic modelling, and electroencephalography. Rather than being uniformly reduced as information accumulates, uncertainty changed its computational form across three interdependent levels: uncertainty within modality-specific semantic representations, bidirectional but asymmetric changes during cross-modal interaction, and uncertainty associated with multisensory convergence. These computational distinctions were accompanied by differentiated but temporally overlapping neural associations. Modality-specific uncertainty was expressed relatively early, whereas cross-modal transformation and convergence were most prominently associated with activity in the N400 range. Critically, both the neural expression and statistical coupling of these computational quantities varied with the semantic information available from gesture and speech. Together, these findings show that multimodal comprehension involves a context-dependent reorganization of uncertainty across interacting representations, providing a computational framework for understanding how coherent meaning emerges from heterogeneous and uncertain information.

item.title: NeuralFieldManifold: Uncovering the Manifold Geometry of Local Field Potentials
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Manifold geometry has become a powerful framework for understanding how the brain organizes high-dimensional neural activity into compact, interpretable structure. To date, however, most theoretical and methodological advances in neural manifold analysis have focused on spiking activity, leaving unresolved a fundamental question: What are the geometric principles governing the dynamics of local field potentials (LFPs)—population level signals reflecting integrated sub-threshold and suprathreshold neural activity that are broadly integral to clinical and brain–computer interface settings. Here, we establish, analytically and empirically, that the lag-embedded dynamics of LFP signals lie on a low-dimensional K-torus, where K directly relates to sustained oscillatory modes present in the signal. Modeling LFPs as bounded autoregressive processes, we show that each oscillatory component contributes an independent circular degree of freedom, while aperiodic 1/f structure and noise contribute only geometric thickness around the manifold without altering its topology. To apply this theory to real nonstationary recordings, we introduce DeepLagField, a physics-informed network that jointly estimates time-varying AR structure and effective model order, with formal guarantees that local toroidal geometry is preserved despite non-stationary nature of neuronal processes. Persistent homology analysis on real recordings reveals topological signatures consistent with the predicted toroidal Betti numbers in primate V1 LFP, rodent hippocampal LFP, and mouse cortical EEG, with varying degrees of agreement across recordings and temporal windows. Crucially, decoding analyses across three distinct neural datasets demonstrate that these geometric structures are not merely descriptive but capture behaviorally relevant information rivaling conventional spectral features. Together, these findings establish a theoretically grounded and empirically validated geometric framework for neural field analysis, extending the manifold perspective beyond spiking activity and offering a complementary language to spectral analysis for understanding and translating population dynamics across neural modalities.

item.title: Embodied Dynamic Causal Modelling: Brain and Cardiac Effective Connectivity
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Brain-body interactions underpin embodied inference and interoception, and are central to both general health and the pathophysiology of mental health disorders. These interactions are orchestrated across a hierarchy extending from the cortex, through the brainstem, to peripheral autonomic effectors. Existing methods either reduce this communication to scalar summaries or lack an invertible biophysical model, and so cannot resolve where in this extended architecture an observed effect originates. To address this, we introduce Embodied Dynamic Causal Modelling, an extension of the generative causal modelling framework that formalises hierarchical message passing across the full brain-body axis. We instantiate the framework for brain-heart interactions with the Brainstem Cardiac Network, a closed-loop neural mass model of brainstem autonomic circuitry and sinoatrial node dynamics. By incorporating five brainstem nuclei, a viscerosensory thalamic relay and the cardiac pacemaker, the network enables estimation of directed effective connectivity across the cortical-brainstem-cardiac axis. As an illustrative case study, representative of the experiments and extended physiological systems that Embodied DCM and the BCN can now interrogate, we applied the framework to simultaneously recorded electroencephalography and electrocardiography during an auditory Go/No-Go paradigm. A multimodal observation model permits joint inversion of electrophysiological and cardiac responses, so that neural and bodily measurements together constrain an account of central and peripheral dynamics. The case study shows how the framework can arbitrate between competing hypotheses about functional cytoarchitecture, distinguishing granular from agranular microcircuits within the viscero-sensorimotor hierarchy. It also shows how time-varying estimates of synaptic efficacy can be recovered alongside continuous latent neuronal dynamics, over extended windows spanning anticipation, target processing and motor inhibition. By linking neural and cardiac signals to a single generative architecture, this work moves the study of brain-heart interactions beyond correlation, providing a framework for testing theories of embodied inference and for identifying circuit-level disruptions in disorders of interoceptive and autonomic regulation.

item.title: Neural circuits, cognition, and behavior in diffuse glioma.
item.description:
Neuro-oncology
Diffuse gliomas arise within and become functionally integrated into neural circuits, establishing bidirectional interactions between malignant cells and the surrounding brain. Neuronal activity promotes glioma growth and progression, while glioma cells remodel the excitability, connectivity, and functional organization of the neural circuits they infiltrate. Pathological excitation-inhibition imbalance can impair cortical information processing, while tumor infiltration simultaneously disrupts, preserves, and induces adaptive reorganization of distributed functional networks. Language processing provides a well defined framework for examining these competing effects because language processing depends on distributed cortical and subcortical networks whose organization can be interrogated using neuroimaging, electrophysiology, and direct cortical stimulation. The pattern and severity of glioma-associated language dysfunction reflect the interaction among tumor location, growth kinetics, molecular and histopathological features, white matter involvement, and the capacity for adaptive redistribution of function within ipsilateral and contralateral networks. Slowly growing gliomas can permit substantial functional reorganization, whereas rapidly infiltrating tumors may constrain the time and biological substrate available for effective network adaptation. In this review, we examine reciprocal glioma-neural circuit interactions, with particular emphasis on the mechanisms of glioma-associated neuronal hyperexcitability and the disruption, preservation, and adaptive remodeling of language networks.

item.title: Hypothalamus-driven brain health through metabolic flexibility.
item.description:
Neuron
Organismal physiology depends on continuous, non-hierarchical communication among cells, tissues, and organs. We argue that this communication rests on metabolic flexibility-the capacity of cells and tissues to adapt substrate use to changing energetic demands-and that the hypothalamus serves as the central hub coordinating this flexibility across the body. Using hypothalamic agouti-related protein (AgRP) and pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) neurons as a model, we show these melanocortin neurons do more than regulate hunger and satiety: by integrating metabolic, hormonal, and immune signals, they shape reward, learning, executive function, and social behavior, while imposing coordinated metabolic states on peripheral tissues. When this flexibility is lost, as with aging or overnutrition, body-brain communication becomes rigid, driving cognitive decline, chronic inflammation, and neurodegenerative disease. We propose that signals from the body are not peripheral modifiers of brain function but fundamental determinants of it, with direct implications for hypothalamus-centered strategies to preserve brain health across the lifespan.

item.title: DPA: Deep Parcellation Analysis for Human Trait Prediction.
item.description:
Neuroinformatics
Mapping individual differences in white matter organization is a central goal of human brain mapping. Atlas-based structural connectome analyses are widely used but are sensitive to anatomical assumptions and may miss fine-grained connectivity patterns. Data-driven fiber clustering mitigates some limitations but typically relies on streamline endpoints, overlooking rich geometric information along full trajectories. In this paper, we introduce Deep Parcellation Analysis (DPA), a geometry-aware framework for white matter parcellation and trait association. DPA samples multiscale geometric features along entire fiber streamlines and encodes them with a Multiscale Fiber AutoEncoder (MFAE) to produce compact latent representations. These enable clustering that preserves intrinsic fiber geometry independently of anatomical atlases, supporting interpretable mapping of connectivity patterns linked to individual differences. Applied to diffusion magnetic resonance imaging data from the Human Connectome Project Young Adult (HCP-YA) cohort, DPA captures white matter substrates underlying language-related cognitive traits. It achieves comparable or superior predictive performance relative to atlas-based and principal parcellation approaches while revealing biologically plausible fiber pathways. Critically, DPA identifies trait-relevant connections missed by endpoint-based methods, emphasizing the importance of full streamline geometry. Overall, DPA demonstrates that deep, geometry-informed parcellation provides a powerful, interpretable approach for linking white matter organization to behavior, advancing structure-function studies in human brain mapping.

item.title: Expertise modifies neural responses to causal inference during language comprehension
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Linguistic communication relies on shared common ground, yet different individuals in a community have specialized semantic knowledge. As a key example, physicians acquire rich knowledge about the causes of illness. An open question is whether such “causal expertise” influences the neural basis of language comprehension. Here we tested the hypothesis that when understanding everyday language like, “Holly used a grimy faucet during her overseas plane ride. Now she has the stomach flu,” medical experts retrieve richer representations in semantic networks of the brain. Physicians (n=16) and age- and education-matched controls (n=16) undergoing fMRI read two-sentence vignettes that elicited implicit causal inferences about illness or object mechanics as well as control vignettes that did not elicit causal inferences. Vignettes were linguistically matched across conditions and were accessible to experts and non-experts alike. Across both groups, causal vignettes about illness engaged a temporoparietal semantic network previously implicated in thinking about animates, i.e., people and animals (precuneus and left temporoparietal junction), whereas causal vignettes about object mechanics engaged a semantic network associated with places and objects. Critically, physicians’ responses in the animacy network were more robust and self-similar, suggesting the activation of richer semantic knowledge. Medical expertise effects were specific to biological inferences rather than mechanical or mental state inferences. By contrast, individually localized frontotemporal language and frontoparietal reasoning networks did not respond preferentially to causally connected sentences or show effects of expertise. Our findings suggest that causal expertise alters neural responses to causal inferences that unfold automatically during language comprehension. Significance statement Shared knowledge is necessary for communication, but what we know about the world varies significantly across individuals. Medical expertise offers a classic example. Relative to other people, medical experts develop a richer understanding of what causes illness. Here we asked whether becoming a “causal expert” alters neural responses during language comprehension. We find that physicians show enhanced responses to causal inferences about illness elicited by language. This expertise effect is specific to semantic networks of the brain that represent knowledge about animate entities, such as people and animals. Our findings suggest that content-specific semantic networks enable causal inferences during language comprehension and are modified by causal expertise, offering new insight into how conceptual variation shapes the neural basis of language.

item.title: An orthographic advantage in spoken word recognition: Behavioral and ERP evidence from cross- and within-modal priming in Korean
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Spoken word recognition may benefit from orthographic information even when spelling differs from surface pronunciation. Korean Hangul preserves spelling across regular phonological changes, allowing us to compare primes matching a target’s written first syllable (orthographic, O), its realized first syllable (phonological, P), or neither (unrelated, U). We report two EEG experiments with independent participant groups, using primed auditory lexical decision on the same 120 disyllabic Korean targets, with within-modal auditory primes (Experiment 1) and cross-modal visual primes (Experiment 2). In both experiments, O primes shortened response latencies and improved accuracy relative to U primes, and produced greater behavioral benefits than P primes. The O–P latency advantage was larger with visual than auditory primes. Phonological latency priming was modest with auditory primes and was not established with visual primes, whereas evidence favored no between-experiment difference in orthographic latency priming. Orthographic relatedness was associated with more positive centro-parietal amplitudes in the N400 window (350–550 ms) in both experiments, without clear evidence of a between-experiment difference. Following visual primes, it also increased fronto-central positivity in the 250–350 ms window, more than following auditory primes. The predicted P200 enhancement was not reliably established. The behavioral O–P advantage was more clearly established than a corresponding N400 difference. The findings suggest that greater surface overlap need not yield greater facilitation and support a role for orthographic relations in spoken word recognition.

item.title: Animal fluency networks and item-based trajectories in people with Parkinson's disease before and after deep brain stimulation surgery.
item.description:
Journal of neuropsychology
Consistent decline in animal fluency occurs in people with Parkinson's disease (PD) post-surgery for Deep Brain Stimulation of the subthalamic nucleus (STN-DBS). Recent findings indicate that patients produce fewer words after (vs. before) surgery. Also, they produce smaller clusters of related animals, fewer switches between clusters, and more frequent (lexical frequency) and earlier-acquired words. In this paper, we further investigated difficulties in lexical retrieval by reporting on word networks (to study the structure of the mental lexicon) and item-based trajectories (to understand how the linguistic characteristics of the task change as the task progresses) of 61 Dutch-speaking individuals diagnosed with PD before and post-surgery for STN-DBS and 40 age and education-matched healthy controls. Word networks contained a higher number of edges and nodes for healthy controls relative to people with PD post-surgery (adjusting for differences in sample size). Also, patients before surgery produced a network with a lower cluster coefficient relative to healthy controls, as well as to people with PD post-surgery. Item-based trajectories showed that both healthy controls and people with PD produced words of increasing complexity as they proceed with the task (e.g., less frequent, acquired later, of higher length). Also, healthy controls showed a steeper increase in the age of acquisition of words across the first ten responses compared to PD post-surgery. The re-emergence of structure (clustering) in word networks post-surgery for STN-DBS and the differences in item-based trajectories (vs. healthy controls) represent novel markers of lexical retrieval that are affected by surgery for STN-DBS and PD.

item.title: Regional lesion burden and chronic post-stroke aphasia severity: Incremental value beyond total lesion volume.
item.description:
Applied neuropsychology. Adult
We examined whether regional lesion burden adds information beyond clinical variables and total lesion volume regarding chronic aphasia severity. This secondary analysis of the Aphasia Recovery Cohort included 195 participants with left-hemisphere stroke, Western Aphasia Battery Aphasia Quotient (AQ) ≤93.8, and assessment ≥180 days after stroke. Lesion burden was quantified in five atlas-defined groups. Partial Spearman correlations were adjusted for age at stroke, sex, time to assessment, and lesion volume, and four ridge-regression models were compared using 30 repetitions of five-fold cross-validation. A sensitivity analysis included participants whose imaging and Western Aphasia Battery assessments were ≤90 days apart (n = 128). Dorsal white-matter burden remained associated with lower AQ after adjustment (partial ρ = -0.261; false-discovery-rate q = 0.002). Adding regional burdens to the clinical-plus-volume model increased mean cross-validated R2 from 0.306 to 0.384 (ΔR2 = 0.078) and reduced mean absolute error from 18.76 to 17.31 AQ points. In the time-restricted sample, R2 increased from 0.312 to 0.442 (ΔR2 = 0.130), with the dorsal association persisting (partial ρ = -0.307). Regional lesion burden adds information beyond lesion volume and supports anatomical characterization of chronic aphasia severity.

item.title: Same Networks, Different Dynamics: Parsimony in Auditory Cognitive Task Processing.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Distinct cognitive states might be supported either by dedicated, task-specific brain networks or by flexible modulation within shared ones, a distinction central to understanding how the brain allocates neural resources. Guided by the principle of parsimony, we hypothesized that both language and numerical cognition, when matched for sensory modality and attentional demand, would engage a common network architecture differentiated primarily through targeted modulation of connectivity strength and temporal dynamics rather than wholesale reconfiguration. We applied a jackknife-based dynamic functional connectivity approach to examine time-varying network engagement during auditory language comprehension and auditory math problem-solving in 172 age- and sex-matched participants from the Human Connectome Project-Young Adult cohort, using the Desikan-Killiany atlas and an 85% participation threshold. Of the significant connections identified, many were retained across both tasks, with 87 connections common to story and math, compared with 26 story-associated and 11 math-associated connections. Rather than indicating a novel shared-core architecture, this overlap is consistent with prior evidence that task functional connectivity is strongly constrained by a common intrinsic connectivity backbone. We therefore used the shared edge set as a common network framework for testing how two modality-matched, but cognitively distinct auditory tasks differ in connectivity strength and temporal variability. Among the 87 shared connections, 84 showed significant task-related differences in mean connectivity strength, indicating that story-math differentiation was expressed primarily through quantitative modulation of shared connections rather than wholesale changes in edge membership. Exploratory rolling-correlation analyses further suggested that some edges may show temporal variability in math-story connectivity correspondence even when mean connectivity strength is similar, highlighting a potential dynamic feature not captured by static connectivity estimates alone. Together, these findings suggest that story and math processing rely on a broadly shared connectivity backbone, while task differentiation emerges through graded modulation of connection strength and, in some cases, temporal variability.

item.title: Reduced magnocellular-biased visual responses are associated with working memory and linguistic difficulties in Chinese developmental dyslexia: A hypothesized visual-cognitive cascade.
item.description:
Cortex; a journal devoted to the study of the nervous system and behavior
Developmental dyslexia (DD) affects 5-10% of children worldwide. Although phonological theories predominate, they may not fully explain reading difficulties in orthographically dense scripts such as Chinese. We investigated whether Chinese children with DD exhibit differences in early visual cortical responses and how these differences relate to reading-related skills. Steady-state visual evoked potentials (ssVEPs) were recorded from 50 children with DD and 50 typically developing controls aged 7-11 years using gratings that preferentially bias magnocellular or parvocellular processing. Global motion perception, visuospatial attention, verbal working memory, and linguistic skills were also assessed. Children with DD showed reduced ssVEP amplitudes to low-spatial-frequency stimuli (partial η2 = .43, p < .001), whereas responses to high-spatial-frequency stimuli were preserved. Among the domains examined, the visual-processing model provided the strongest within-sample discrimination between groups (Nagelkerke R2 = .68), with low-spatial-frequency ssVEP amplitude as its only significant visual predictor. Exploratory cross-sectional mediation analyses identified significant indirect associations between ssVEP amplitude and linguistic skills through verbal working memory. For phonological awareness, the indirect association was significant, whereas the corresponding direct association was not; for morphological awareness, both associations remained significant. Visuospatial-attention differences were limited to retrospective selection from working memory rather than initial attentional orienting. For most measures, age-related associations did not differ detectably between groups. These findings are compatible with a hypothesized visual-cognitive cascade involving early visual cortical processing, working memory, and reading-related difficulties. However, the cross-sectional design does not establish temporal or causal relationships; longitudinal and intervention studies are needed to test the proposed model.

item.title: Human iEEG recordings during audiovisual speech violations support and extend predictive routing models.
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
Rather than constantly reconstructing the world solely through sensory input, predictive processing theories posit that the brain utilizes predictions maintained as internal representations to guide sensory processing. An emerging model, predictive routing, proposes that an interplay between neuronal gamma (40-150 Hz) and alpha-beta (10-30 Hz) rhythms implements a dynamic mechanism for predictive processing. Namely, predictions enhance alpha-beta oscillations that suppress gamma activity during the processing of predicted inputs. While this model is supported by animal studies, its validity has not been fully explored within the human brain. The present study addresses this by leveraging human intracranial EEG (iEEG) recordings across superior temporal and prefrontal/premotor areas of seven presurgical epilepsy patients during an audiovisual speech paradigm. We calculated iEEG power in the theta, alpha-beta, and high gamma bands during simple auditory deviance, multisensory integration, and a condition where an incongruent visual cue (lip movements) clashed with an auditory stimulus (a syllable), creating audiovisual incongruence that can elicit the McGurk illusion. Results revealed increased high-gamma and decreased alpha-beta power in the superior temporal cortex in response to auditory deviance and the McGurk condition, while frontal areas, despite reflecting a similar decrease in alpha-beta power, did not present this high gamma prediction error signal. Instead, the theta band revealed a strong prediction error signal in the McGurk condition, consistent with theories on the role of theta in reorganizing cortical networks. These results both support and extend existing predictive routing models for human-specific forms of predictive processing.

item.title: Capturing the Attentional Trade-off between Speech Planning and Comprehension.
item.description:
Journal of cognitive neuroscience
In conversation, future speakers often plan speech simultaneously with comprehension, which means that they must divide attentional resources between these processes. In this EEG study, we used responses to linguistic attention probes (i.e., syllable "BA" presented during spoken sentences) to track temporal variations in attention to comprehension. Participants were asked to listen to prerecorded sentences with expected or unexpected sentence-final words. Each sentence was presented twice, once with and once without the attention probe starting 100 msec after the target word onset. Participants saw a picture 50 msec before the target word. Depending on the test block (picture naming or button press), participants either named the picture or pressed the space bar, both after an 850-msec delay. The probes elicited a negative potential approximately 100 msec after probe onset (i.e., an attention probe effect) in all probe conditions. Unexpectedly, neither word expectancy nor speech planning influenced the timing or strength of the attention probe effect. This indicates that expectancy of words in Dutch does not affect the allocation of attention toward these words 100 msec after their onset (i.e., the time of the probe presentation). Interestingly, engaging in speech planning does not seem to divert attentional resources away from comprehension at the moment of probe presentation. These findings imply that listeners are able to effectively distribute their attentional resources between comprehension and speech planning and carry out these processes at the same time. Considering these unexpected findings, using attention probes might not be the best approach to capture variations in temporal attention in dual-task paradigms.

item.title: Distinct Patterns of Syntactic Errors Doubly Dissociate in Chronic Poststroke Aphasia.
item.description:
Journal of cognitive neuroscience
The lesion correlates of syntactic deficits in aphasia remain poorly understood. Previous studies have suggested that distinct error types in expressive syntax may be associated with damage to different brain regions, but the specific lesion correlates of these errors have not been fully delineated. To address this gap, we analyzed spontaneous speech samples from individuals with chronic aphasia, categorizing errors into hierarchical (paragrammatic-like) and linearization (agrammatic-like) errors. Lesion-symptom mapping was conducted to identify brain regions associated with these error types. Lesion clusters in the medial superior temporal sulcus and inferior parietal lobe were associated with hierarchical errors, whereas frontal lesions, including those in the inferior and middle frontal lobe, were associated with linearization errors. These results provide support for a two-stage model of syntactic encoding, with distinct neural correlates for hierarchical and linearization processes. Our findings suggest that distinct brain regions contribute to different stages of syntactic encoding. Hierarchical processing seems to be supported by posterior temporal-parietal regions, whereas linearization seems to be supported by frontal regions. These results suggest that the diagnosis and treatment of aphasia could take into account the existence of distinct syntactic production deficits resulting from different patterns of brain damage.

item.title: Memory Traces Reflect How They Were Last Accessed.
item.description:
Journal of cognitive neuroscience
Episodic memories are known to change with each act of retrieval. We hypothesize that accessing semantic knowledge in different ways during episodic retrieval-from unique perceptual features to taxonomic and thematic context-shapes how those memories are subsequently represented during recognition. In this fMRI study, human participants learned novel word-image pairs and underwent re-exposure that required accessing semantic knowledge at one of three different levels: item, category, or theme. Participants then completed a recognition task. Although behavioral memory performance was matched across conditions, neural activity during recognition varied based on prior semantic access history. Recognition patterns could be classified according to prior semantic access in early visual cortex, ventral temporal cortex, and the hippocampus for remembered concepts. A whole-brain searchlight analysis revealed bilateral clusters along the ventral visual stream where semantic access history was decodable. To further characterize how prior semantic access history shaped neural representations during recognition, we tested whether memories accessed at the same semantic level were expressed more similarly or distinctly in the brain. Category-level access increased similarity among items in early visual cortex, whereas item-level access led to more differentiated representations in the visual word form area. Together, these findings show that how we access semantic knowledge during episodic retrieval leaves measurable traces in subsequent neural representations, revealing how semantic-episodic interactions shape memory representations.

item.title: Intracranial Evidence for the Cerebellum's Role in Semantic Processing.
item.description:
Journal of cognitive neuroscience
Language impairments in patients with cerebellar damage or dysfunction strongly implicate the cerebellum in language processing but the nature, timing, and specificity of its contributions are unclear. A clinical trial of cerebellar stimulation for motor recovery after middle cerebral artery stroke provided a rare opportunity to record invasive, intracranial local field potential activity from the cerebellar dentate nucleus of eight patients during language processing. Patients performed semantic priming tasks that either discouraged or encouraged semantic predictions. We found evidence for communication between the dentate nucleus and frontal scalp EEG sites in the alpha band when semantic predictions were violated. This did not occur when semantic predictions were fulfilled or when prediction violations were nonlinguistic in nature. This language-specific activity occurred in the N400 window where semantic processing of a visually presented word takes place. These data point to a linguistic feedback function that could help to account for the language deficits observed in diseases and disorders involving the cerebellum.

item.title: Early Emergence of Cultural Differences in Audiovisual Speech Perception.
item.description:
Developmental science
Integrating auditory and visual cues is a hallmark of human speech perception, yet adults from East Asian backgrounds show less reliance on visual speech than their Western counterparts. The origins of this cultural difference, however, remain unknown. To investigate whether this divergence is established early in infancy, we examined audiovisual integration in 6- to 12-month-old White Canadian (n = 111) and Chinese (n = 115) infants using a novel paradigm measuring their perception of the McGurk effect. Across four experiments, we found a clear developmental divergence: Canadian infants showed a stable McGurk effect from 6 months onward, whereas Chinese infants showed a more protracted developmental trajectory, a cultural pattern that was further highlighted when their integration was challenged by other-race faces. These findings provide the first direct evidence that cultural differences in multisensory speech perception are established within the first year of life, suggesting that the brain's strategy for binding sight and sound is shaped by early experience, with broad implications for theories of language acquisition and developmental science.

item.title: Computation or Weight Adaptation? Rethinking the Role of Plasticity in Learning.
item.description:
Cognitive science
The human brain is an adaptive learning system that can generalize to new tasks and unfamiliar environments. The traditional view is that such adaptive behavior requires a structural change of the learning system (e.g., via neural plasticity). In this work, we use artificial neural networks, specifically large language models (LLMs), to challenge this traditional view and suggest that such adaptive behavior can be also achieved solely through computation if the learning system is sufficiently trained. We focus on statistical learning paradigms. These require identifying underlying regularities in seemingly arbitrary word sequences and are primarily considered to require neural plasticity. LLMs can capture arbitrary structures without requiring weight adaptation, even though these structures carry no semantic content and lie far from the natural language distribution on which the models were trained. Our work provides novel insights into the role of plasticity in learning, demonstrating that sufficiently trained learning systems are highly flexible, adapting to new tasks and environments solely through computation, much more than previously acknowledged. Furthermore, our work opens the door for future research to use deep learning models to conjure hypotheses about the brain.

item.title: Lexico-Semantic and Morphosyntactic Skills in Individuals With Parkinson's Disease: A Scoping Review.
item.description:
International journal of language & communication disorders
Purpose This scoping review examines lexico-semantic and morphosyntactic skills in English-speaking individuals with Parkinson's disease (PD) using behavioral and neuroimaging data to inform clinical assessment and intervention. Method Following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, observational case-control studies published between 2004 and 2024 were retrieved from PubMed, PsycINFO, Web of Science, Scopus and ERIC. Thirty-nine studies met inclusion criteria. Methodological quality was evaluated using the Joanna Briggs Institute Checklist for Case-Control Studies. Results Lexico-semantic impairments in PD are characterized by deficits in semantic fluency, action-verb retrieval, and figurative-language processing, particularly under higher cognitive load. Individuals with PD show reduced efficiency in lexical access, difficulty shifting between semantic categories, and weaker inhibition of competing meanings. Morphosyntactic studies similarly report slower processing and lower accuracy for syntactically complex sentences. Conclusion Linguistic impairments in PD are best understood as a dynamic interaction between linguistic demands and domain-general cognitive resources, emerging most clearly under conditions of increased cognitive load. This pattern positions language as a sensitive indicator of broader cognitive vulnerability within the communication profile of PD, with direct implications for assessment and clinical practice. What this paper adds What is already known on the subject Language impairments are a well-recognized non-motor feature of PD and can significantly affect communication and quality of life. Previous studies have reported lexico-semantic and morphosyntactic difficulties in PD, but findings are scattered across heterogeneous tasks and study designs, with no synthesis examining these domains together. What this study adds to the existing knowledge This scoping review synthesizes evidence from behavioral and neuroimaging studies and shows that language difficulties in PD are most consistently observed under conditions of increased cognitive or processing demand, particularly in high-load contexts. Lexico-semantic impairments emerge reliably in such high-load contexts, while morphosyntactic difficulties appear to reflect vulnerability to processing demands rather than a generalized grammatical deficit. The review also demonstrates that methodological variability, such as cognitive screening practices, influences how language abilities are characterized across studies. What are the potential or clinical implications of this work? Language impairments affecting lexico-semantic and morphosyntactic processing constitute a meaningful component of the communication profile in PD and should be considered alongside speech and voice symptoms in clinical assessment. Incorporating cognitive-linguistic evaluation may support a more comprehensive understanding of communication difficulties in individuals with PD.

item.title: Event-Related Potential Components and the Lexical Decision Task in Greek-Speaking Children With and Without Reading Difficulties.
item.description:
Dyslexia (Chichester, England)
The present study examined neurocognitive differences in visual word processing between children with reading difficulties (RD) and chronological-age-matched controls (CA) using event-related potentials (ERPs) during a lexical decision task. Participants were Grade 3 and Grade 6 children (ages 7.6-12.1 years) who were required to discriminate real words from orthographically similar pseudowords. ERP analyses focused on the N200 and N400 components, which are thought to reflect early stages of visual word processing and later processes involved in lexical access and stimulus evaluation. The results showed that the Grade 3 RD group exhibited significantly higher Ν200 amplitudes than their CA controls, suggesting less efficient early processing of the presented stimuli. However, no differences in the N200 were observed between the Grade 6 groups. Children with RD in both grades exhibited reduced N400 amplitudes compared to their counterparts, suggesting differences in the neural processes supporting word recognition. These findings contribute to a clearer understanding of the temporal dynamics of written word processing in children with RD in transparent orthographies and highlight the value of ERP measures for examining neurocognitive mechanisms underlying reading development.

item.title: Co-constructed Emotion: A Collective Predictive Coding Theory of Interoception and Social Symbol Sharing
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Emotion is both a psychological phenomenon rooted in physiological fluctuations and a socially constructed phenomenon shaped by language and culture. However, traditional psychological constructivism has remained confined to individual brain processes, while social constructivism has lacked a bottom-up computational mechanism explaining how language and culture emerge from bodily emotional substrates and dynamically evolve. To bridge this theoretical gap, this paper proposes the Theory of Co-constructed Emotion (TCoE) via Collective Predictive Coding (CPC), a framework coupling physiological regulation with social symbol sharing within a single active inference formulation. We extend the conventional CPC model by explicitly incorporating interoception---which is indispensable for modeling emotion from a physiological perspective---into each agent's generative model, alongside exteroception and internal and external representations. In TCoE, the co-construction of emotion is described as a dual inference process: an internal loop of allostasis regulating individual bodily states, and a social loop of communication sharing emotional concepts with others. These loops mutually minimize prediction errors mediated by shared symbols (emotion words). We argue that this theoretical framework 1) aligns with psychological findings on emotional contagion and concept formation, 2) enables constructive verification in multi-agent robotic systems, and 3) provides a computational redefinition of psychiatric conditions such as alexithymia as a disconnection between interoception and social symbols. Thus, we offer a novel computational foundation for emotion research that unifies individual embodiment and social symbol systems.

item.title: MicroRNA-loaded extracellular vesicles: Mechanisms and therapeutic potential in senescence and aging.
item.description:
Mechanisms of ageing and development
Cellular senescence is a biological process characterized by stable cell cycle arrest that contributes to tumor suppression and tissue remodeling but can also promote aging-associated dysfunction when senescent cells persist and accumulate. Senescent cells influence neighboring and distant tissues through the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), of which extracellular vesicles (EVs) are an increasingly recognized component. This review examines how microRNAs (miRNAs) carried by EVs regulate senescence and ageing. miRNAs are key post-transcriptional regulators of senescence, particularly within the p53/p21Cip1 and p16INK4a /Rb tumor suppressor pathways. Selective sorting into EVs allows these molecules to act over long distances. EV-miRNAs have dual roles: anti-senescent miRNAs such as miR-17-5p, miR-146a and miR-378a-3p promote rejuvenation, whereas pro-senescent miRNAs including miR-34a, miR-21 and miR-27a propagate ageing. Hypothalamic neural stem cell-derived miRNAs maintain transcriptional homeostasis and suppress senescence across the brain, and their age-related decline contributes to neurodegeneration. miRNAs in small EVs from young plasma rejuvenate multiple organ systems and extend lifespan in mice, while adipocyte-derived miR-27a spreads metabolic dysfunction to distant tissues. Together, EV-miRNAs are an emerging component of the intercellular networks regulating cellular senescence and aging, and their selective sorting, intercellular transfer, and modulation of senescence-associated pathways provide opportunities for therapeutic development and biomarker discovery.

item.title: From Images and Words to Modality-Independent Semantic Representations: When and Where They Emerge
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Conceptual knowledge can be accessed from different modalities, such as seeing an image or reading a written word. While prior neuroimaging studies implicate anterior temporal cortex in modality-independent semantic representations, when and how representations evoked by images and words converge onto a modality-independent code remains unclear. Moreover, evidence for modality-independent category representations comes largely from tasks that explicitly required semantic processing, leaving open whether such representations emerge when semantic category and stimulus modality are task-irrelevant. We magnetoencephalography (MEG) to determine when and where modality-independent semantic category representations emerge across images and words when participants (n = 32) encoded six-item sequences containing an exemplar of six semantic categories counterbalanced across positions and reported the ordinal position of a probed item. Decoding performance was above chance for all categories in each modality from approximately 70 ms relative to item presentation. Generalization peaked at similar latencies for the two modalities (∼520-530 ms), where image and word classifiers had the most similar coefficients. In both transfer directions, activity elicited by images generalized mostly to later activity elicited by words, and a given period of the image response shared its category code with a longer period of the word response. Source-space decoding around the peak of generalization identified the same regions for both transfer directions: left and right anterior temporal lobe, perisylvian cortex (more extensive in the left hemisphere), right visual cortex, and bilateral orbitofrontal cortex, indicating a modality-independent category code distributed across the cortex.

item.title: Fixel-wise differences in White Matter Fiber-bundle Cross-section identified in Children who Stutter.
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
UNLABELLED: Developmental stuttering has been repeatedly linked to decreased white matter integrity and structural connectivity differences in major white matter tracts. Prior diffusion-weighted MRI studies reporting such white matter structural differences involved voxel-averaged tensor measures (e.g., fractional anisotropy (FA)). A well-acknowledged limitation of this approach, however, has been that it cannot resolve distinct fiber populations within crossing-fiber regions. Fixel-based analysis addresses this limitation by quantifying individual fiber populations within a voxel and providing complementary measures of fiber density (FD), fiber-bundle cross-section (FC), and their combined measure (FDC).
