Here we applied Fixel-based analysis to diffusion MRI data from 171 children aged 3-13 years, including 84 children who stutter and 87 typically developing controls, to test whether white-matter differences associated with developmental stuttering were expressed as differences in FD, FC, and FDC and whether these measures show group-specific age-related patterns. We evaluated this at both the whole-brain level and within a priori white-matter tracts. FC, but not FD or FDC, showed significant Group and Group × Age effects, indicating that white-matter differences were primarily expressed in fiber-bundle macrostructure. Tract-of-interest analyses identified developmental differences in bilateral arcuate fasciculus FC that remained significant across tracts, with controls showing greater age-related increases in FC than children who stutter. Additional FC differences were observed across corticospinal and thalamocortical pathways, although these tract-wise effects were less robust to across-tract correction. These findings suggest that white-matter differences in developmental stuttering are prominently expressed in fiber-bundle macrostructure rather than fiber density and highlight divergent development of bilateral arcuate pathways. FBA provides fiber-specific information that complements conventional tensor-based diffusion measures and may improve characterization of white-matter development in childhood stuttering. SIGNIFICANCE STATEMENT: Developmental stuttering has repeatedly been associated with white-matter differences, but conventional diffusion measures cannot readily distinguish changes in individual fiber populations within regions containing crossing fibers. Using Fixel-based analysis in children who stutter, we show that these differences are primarily expressed in fiber-bundle cross-section rather than fiber density, implicating macrostructural differences in white-matter organization. The strongest tract-wise developmental effects were observed bilaterally in the arcuate fasciculus, a major pathway supporting auditory-motor integration, where children who stutter showed divergent age-related trajectories relative to typically developing children. These findings provide a fiber-specific perspective on the neurodevelopmental basis of stuttering and refine the interpretation of white-matter differences previously identified using conventional diffusion imaging.

item.title: Item-specific clustering of high gamma-band activity on theta phase during speech categorization
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Theta-gamma phase-amplitude coupling (PAC) has been proposed as a mechanism for separating neural representations in time. Although item-specific PAC has been reported, its role in perception remains unclear. Notably, previous work has shown that theta phase can bias perception, raising the question whether such biases are linked to phase-specific gamma activity. Here, we investigated whether phase-dependent perceptual biases are accompanied by item-specific theta-gamma PAC. We presented ambiguous speech sounds that could be interpreted as either /da/ or /ga/ in patients with epilepsy implanted with intracranial electrocorticography. We found that pre-stimulus theta phase predicted both the neural and perceptual response, with /da/ and /ga/ tuned channels exhibiting gamma activity clustering at distinct theta phases. These findings suggest that neural and perceptual biases stem from phase-specific pre-activation of item-specific neural representations. They demonstrate the generalizability of the theta-gamma code, shaping behavior and enhancing representational capacity.

item.title: Decomposing Parts of Speech: Neural Encoding of Semantic and Grammatical Dimensions and Their Combinational Structure
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Conventional part-of-speech (PoS) labels such as nouns, verbs and adjectives conflate lexical-semantic roots, grammatical functions, and their combinations, making it unclear whether neural sensitivity to PoS reflects either dimension or the way they are combined. We adopted Croft's typological framework to decompose major PoS classes into semantic root type and grammatical function and define prototypical nouns, verbs, and adjectives through the prototypical mappings between semantic root and grammatical function. We fitted time-resolved encoding models to magnetoencephalography (MEG) data from three participants who each listened to approximately ten hours of narrative speech. We examined the unique predictive contributions of semantic root, grammatical function, their interaction, and a binary prototypicality predictor, and whether the three prototypes exhibited distinct neural response dynamics. Semantic root and grammatical function contributed independently to neural responses during naturalistic language comprehension, with additional contributions from their interaction beyond the main effects. Root effects were predominantly left-lateralized, function effects were more bilateral, and interaction effects were concentrated in the left temporal and temporoparietal cortex, with overlap in left temporal regions. Further analyses revealed significant neural sensitivity to the distinction between prototypical and nonprototypical combinations in two of the three datasets. Prototypical nouns and verbs showed distinct coefficient time courses in all three participants, most consistently in left superior temporal cortex, whereas adjective-related contrasts were less consistent. These within-participant findings support a decompositional account of neural word-class sensitivity involving semantic, grammatical, and the mappings between them within distributed, partially overlapping cortical networks.

item.title: Interpretable embeddings of speech explain and enhance the brain encoding performance of audio models.
item.description:
PLoS computational biology
Speech foundation models (SFMs) are increasingly hailed as powerful computational models of human speech perception. However, since their representations are inherently black-box, it remains unclear what drives their alignment with brain responses. To remedy this, we built linear encoding models from six interpretable feature families: mel-spectrogram, Gabor filter bank features, speech presence, phonetic, syntactic, and semantic features, and contextualized embeddings from three state-of-the-art SFMs (Whisper, HuBERT, WavLM), quantifying electrocorticography (ECoG) response variance shared between feature classes. Variance-partitioning analyses revealed several key insights: First, the SFMs' alignment with the brain can be mostly accounted for by their ability to learn and encode simple interpretable speech features. Second, SFMs exhibit a systematic trade-off between encoding of brain-relevant low-level and high-level features across layers. Finally, our results show that SFMs learn brain-relevant semantics which cannot be accounted for by lower-level speech features, with this capacity increasing with model size and context length. Together, our findings suggest a principled approach to build more interpretable, accurate, and efficient encoding models of the brain by augmenting SFM embeddings with interpretable features.

item.title: Delineating neural contributions to electroencephalogram-based speech decoding.
item.description:
Journal of neural engineering
Objective . Speech brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have emerged as a pivotal technology in facilitating communication for individuals with speech impairments. Utilizing electroencephalography (EEG) for noninvasive speech BCIs offers an accessible and affordable solution, potentially benefiting a broader audience. However, EEG-based speech decoding remains controversial especially for overt speech, due to difficulties in separating speech-related neural activities from myoelectric potential artifacts generated during articulation. Moreover, because paradigms for collecting covert speech data are inherently less scalable than those for overt speech, whether the neural dynamics underlying EEG-based decoding of overt speech are also present during covert speech remains an open and practically important question.Approach . Here we aim to delineate the extent of the neural contributions to EEG-based speech decoding, and the degree to which the underlying neural dynamics are shared across overt and covert speech, by employing Explainable AI techniques to a convolutional neural network predicting spoken words based on signals obtained by ultra-high-density (uhd)-EEG.Main results . We found that electrode-wise contributions to the decoding cannot be explained by their mutual information with electromyography (EMG). Furthermore, contributing periods of speech to EEG-based decoding are distinct from those to decoding solely relying on EMG. Contributing periods of EEG-based decoding partially overlapped between overt and minimally overt speech. Notably, the denoising process successfully enhanced the decoding contribution from electrodes within speech-related brain areas for all speech conditions.Significance . Altogether, our findings support the idea that, with appropriate preprocessing, EEG becomes a valuable tool for decoding spoken words based on underlying neural activities.

item.title: The impact of pruning iterations on Arcuate Fasciculus morphometry and diffusion features in right-handed adults.
item.description:
Radiological physics and technology
To evaluate the utility of a pruning method in refining tractography and to examine the Arcuate Fasciculus (AF) morphometry and diffusion metrics in right-handed adults. Thirty-two healthy, right-handed adults underwent DTI on a 1.5T MRI system. Q-space diffeomorphic reconstruction was performed on a single-shell DTI dataset, and the AF was automatically tracked. Topology-Informed Pruning (TIP) was applied to reduce false-positive streamlines across varying numbers of iterations. Morphometry and diffusion metrics of the bilateral AF were extracted. The associations between these metrics and the number of iterations were evaluated using correlation analysis. The protocol-specific TIP threshold was identified as the knee point using the Kneedle algorithm. Differences in the morphometry and diffusion metrics of the selection AF tractometry by sex and hemisphere were also examined. A pFDR < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. TIP-based pruning was associated with improved tract delineation through the reduction of spurious streamlines. The number of pruning iterations affected the AF's morphometry and diffusion metrics. The selected TIP threshold was 8, and TIPs greater than 8 yielded stable values with minimal variability. Significant differences between hemispheres were observed in diffusion metrics except quantitative anisotropy (QA). For morphometry metrics, significant differences were identified in the number of tracts, span, and curl (pFDR < 0.05). No significant sex-related differences were found after FDR correction. Pruning iterations affect the visualization of AF in the protocol-specific population of right-handed adults. The number of pruning iterations selected should be carefully determined with full awareness and consideration.

item.title: The effect of acupuncture-rehabilitation therapy on brain functional plasticity in motor aphasia after ischemic stroke: a randomized clinical neuroimaging trial.
item.description:
Brain imaging and behavior
Motor aphasia is the most prevalent type of aphasia following ischemic stroke (IS). This study aims to evaluate the therapeutic efficacy and underlying neural mechanisms of acupuncture-rehabilitation (A-R) therapy on motor aphasia after IS. Twenty-six patients with post-IS motor aphasia were randomly assigned to either the A-R group or the Conventional Rehabilitation (CR) group in a 1:1 ratio, and matched by age and gender with 26 healthy controls (HCs). The CR group received standard treatment and language training, while the A-R group additionally underwent scalp acupoint cluster acupuncture. Behavioral assessments and Blood Oxygenation Level Dependent functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (BOLD-fMRI) scans were conducted before and after the four-week intervention to evaluate therapeutic outcomes and underlying mechanisms. Compared to HCs, patients exhibited decreased Amplitude of Low Frequency Fluctuations (ALFF) in the right precuneus (p < 0.05) and reduced Regional Homogeneity (ReHo) in the left precuneus/postcentral gyrus (p < 0.05). Enhanced functional connectivity (FC) was observed in regions including the left Broca's area and right superior temporal gyrus, left Broca's area and right inferior frontal orbitalis gyrus, left Broca's area and right precentral gyrus, left Broca's area and right postcentral gyrus (p < 0.05). After intervention, significant improvements were observed in Aphasia Quotient (AQ) scores and sub-item performance in both patient groups (p < 0.05), with the A-R group showing greater gains in AQ and spontaneous speech scores compared to the CR group (p < 0.05). FMRI results indicated a significant increase in mean ALFF (mALFF) in the left inferior temporal gyrus after A-R treatment (p < 0.05) compared to before, and higher szReHo in the left anterior central gyrus compared to the CR group (p < 0.05). FC between the left Broca's area and right precentral gyrus decreased in the A-R group (p < 0.05). Additionally, a negative correlation was observed between the right anterior central gyrus and listening comprehension (r = -0.574, p = 0.020). The findings suggest that both A-R and CR therapies enhance language function in patients with motor aphasia post-IS, with A-R therapy demonstrating superior efficacy. The therapeutic mechanism of A-R likely involves activating left hemisphere brain regions, suppressing right hemisphere activity, and restoring hemispheric balance to facilitate functional recovery.
